q: The force on a straight wire of length L carrying current I in a uniform magnetic field B is F = I(L × B). The direction of this force is always:
o: Perpendicular to both the wire and the field
Halfway between the wire and the field
x: A vector product is perpendicular to both of the vectors multiplied, so F is at right angles to both L and B. It is never along the field or along the wire.

q: A flat coil of area 0.2 m² is in a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T. The plane of the coil makes an angle of 30° with the field. The magnetic flux through the coil is (sin 30° = 0.5, cos 30° ≈ 0.87):
x: Φ = BA cos θ with θ the angle between B and the normal to the coil. The plane is at 30° to B, so the normal is at 60°: Φ = 0.5 × 0.2 × cos 60° = 0.05 Wb. Using cos 30° (the angle with the plane) gives 0.087 Wb.

q: A horizontal straight wire 0.5 m long has a mass of 20 g. It lies in a horizontal uniform magnetic field of 0.4 T at right angles to the wire. The current needed for the magnetic force to support the wire's weight is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
x: BIL = mg, so I = mg/(BL) = (0.02 × 10)/(0.4 × 0.5) = 0.2/0.2 = 1 A. Taking 20 g as 0.2 kg gives 10 A; leaving out g gives 0.1 A.

q: A rectangular loop of wire carrying a steady current is placed in a uniform magnetic field. The net magnetic force on the whole loop is:
o: Zero, although the loop may experience a torque
Largest when the plane of the loop is perpendicular to the field
Equal to BIL for each side, added together
x: In a uniform field the forces on opposite sides of a closed loop are equal and opposite, so they add to zero. They can still form a couple, which is why a coil turns in a motor or meter.

q: A straight current-carrying wire at 30° to a uniform magnetic field experiences a force F. The wire is turned until it is at 90° to the field, with the same current. The force on it becomes:
x: F = BIL sin θ, so the force goes from BIL × 0.5 to BIL × 1: it doubles to 2F. Using cos instead of sin would give a smaller force.

q: A wire bent into a semicircle of radius 0.1 m carries a current of 5 A. A uniform magnetic field of 0.2 T acts perpendicular to the plane of the semicircle. The resultant force on the semicircular wire is (π ≈ 3.14):
x: In a uniform field a curved wire feels the same resultant force as a straight wire joining its ends, here the diameter 2r = 0.2 m: F = BIL = 0.2 × 5 × 0.2 = 0.2 N. Using the arc length πr = 0.314 m gives 0.314 N, but the sideways parts of the arc cancel.

q: The total magnetic flux through any closed surface, for example a sphere drawn around a bar magnet, is:
o: Equal to the pole strength of the magnet
Zero, because magnetic field lines form closed loops
Largest when the magnet is at the centre of the sphere
Equal to B multiplied by the surface area
x: Every field line that leaves a closed surface also enters it, because magnetic lines have no beginning or end (no single magnetic poles). So the outward and inward flux cancel and the total is zero.

q: Which physical quantity has the SI unit N m A⁻¹?
x: 1 T = 1 N A⁻¹ m⁻¹, and flux Φ = BA has unit T m² = N A⁻¹ m⁻¹ × m² = N m A⁻¹, which is the weber. Flux density itself is N A⁻¹ m⁻¹.

q: The SI unit of the permeability of free space, μ₀, can be written as:
x: From B = μ₀I/(2πr), μ₀ = 2πrB/I, so its unit is T × m / A = T m A⁻¹, matching μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹.

q: A long solenoid is wound with 20 turns per centimetre and carries a current of 0.5 A. The magnetic field inside it is (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹):
x: n = 20 per cm = 2000 per m, so B = μ₀nI = 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 2000 × 0.5 = 4π × 10⁻⁴ T. Using n = 20 per metre gives 4π × 10⁻⁶ T.

q: For a long straight current-carrying wire, the magnetic field B is plotted against 1/r, where r is the distance from the wire. The graph is:
o: A straight line through the origin
A straight line with a negative gradient
x: B = (μ₀I/2π) × (1/r), so B is directly proportional to 1/r: a straight line through the origin with gradient μ₀I/2π. B against r itself would be the falling curve.

q: A long straight vertical wire carries a current flowing upward. Seen from above, looking down along the wire, the magnetic field lines around it are:
o: Clockwise circles centred on the wire
Anticlockwise circles centred on the wire
Straight lines parallel to the wire
Straight lines pointing away from the wire
x: By the right-hand grip rule, with the thumb along the current (upward, towards an observer above), the fingers curl anticlockwise as seen from above. A downward current would give clockwise circles.

q: Two long parallel wires 10 cm apart carry currents of 5 A each in opposite directions. The magnetic field at the point midway between them is (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹):
x: Each wire gives B = μ₀I/(2πr) = 2 × 10⁻⁷ × 5 / 0.05 = 2 × 10⁻⁵ T at the midpoint. With opposite currents the two fields there point the same way, so they add to 4 × 10⁻⁵ T. Zero would be the answer for currents in the same direction.

q: A long solenoid is stretched to twice its length. The number of turns, the radius and the current stay the same. The magnetic field inside it becomes:
o: One quarter of its original value
x: B = μ₀nI with n = N/L. Doubling L with N fixed halves n, so B halves. Thinking only the total number of turns matters gives unchanged.

q: A long solenoid carries a steady current. An electron is fired along the axis of the solenoid, inside it. The magnetic force on the electron is:
o: Directed radially outward, so it spirals to the windings
Equal to evB, so it moves in a circle
Zero, so it keeps moving along the axis at constant speed
Directed along the axis, so it speeds up
x: Inside a long solenoid the field is uniform and along the axis, so the electron's velocity is parallel to B. Then F = evB sin 0° = 0, and it moves in a straight line at constant speed.

q: A charged particle moves through a uniform magnetic field. The work done on it by the magnetic force is:
o: Zero, because the force is always perpendicular to the velocity
Positive, because the force speeds the particle up
Negative, because the force slows the particle down
Equal to qvB times the distance moved
x: F = q(v × B) is always at right angles to v, so it does no work (W = Fd cos 90° = 0). The particle's speed and kinetic energy stay constant; only its direction changes.

q: An electron moves at 2 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ at an angle of 30° to a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T. The magnetic force on it is (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, sin 30° = 0.5, cos 30° ≈ 0.87):
x: F = evB sin θ = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 2 × 10⁶ × 0.5 × 0.5 = 8 × 10⁻¹⁴ N. Leaving out sin 30° gives 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ N; using cos 30° gives about 1.4 × 10⁻¹³ N.

q: A particle with charge-to-mass ratio q/m = 10⁸ C kg⁻¹ moves in a circle at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of 0.1 T. The time for one revolution is:
x: T = 2πm/(qB) = 2π / (10⁸ × 0.1) = 2π × 10⁻⁷ s. Leaving out 2π gives 10⁻⁷ s, which is 1/ω.

q: A velocity selector has uniform electric and magnetic fields at right angles to each other and to a beam of particles. Which particles pass straight through undeflected?
o: Only those with speed E/B, whatever their charge or mass
Only positive particles with speed E/B
Only particles of one particular mass
x: No deflection needs qE = qvB, so v = E/B; q cancels, and mass does not appear. For a negative particle both forces reverse together and still balance. Faster particles are pushed aside by the larger magnetic force.

q: Ions pass undeflected through a velocity selector with E = 1 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹ and B = 0.1 T. They then enter a region where only a uniform magnetic field of 0.1 T acts, at right angles to their velocity, and move in a circle of radius 1 cm. Their charge-to-mass ratio is:
x: From the selector, v = E/B = 10⁴/0.1 = 10⁵ m s⁻¹. In the field r = mv/(qB), so q/m = v/(rB) = 10⁵/(0.01 × 0.1) = 10⁸ C kg⁻¹. Leaving r in centimetres gives 10⁶ C kg⁻¹.

q: Electrons accelerated from rest through a p.d. V move in a circle of radius r at right angles to a uniform magnetic field. If the accelerating p.d. is made 4V, with the same field, the radius becomes:
x: eV = ½mv² gives v ∝ √V, and r = mv/(eB) ∝ v, so r ∝ √V. Four times V gives √4 = 2 times r. Forgetting the square root gives 4r.

q: An electron moves horizontally towards the east through a uniform magnetic field that points vertically downward. The direction of the magnetic force on the electron is:
x: For a positive charge F is along v × B: east × downward points north. The electron's charge is negative, so its force is the opposite way: south. Forgetting the negative charge gives north.

q: The total force F = qE + q(v × B) on a charge moving through both an electric and a magnetic field is called the:
x: The combined electric and magnetic force on a moving charge is the Lorentz force. The Coulomb force is only the electric part qE; emf is not a force at all.

q: An ideal ammeter should have:
o: Zero resistance, and be connected in series
Infinite resistance, and be connected in parallel
Zero resistance, and be connected in parallel
Infinite resistance, and be connected in series
x: An ammeter goes in series so the current to be measured passes through it, and it should have no resistance so it does not reduce that current. The ideal voltmeter is the opposite: infinite resistance, in parallel.

q: An AVO meter (multimeter) is used to measure:
x: AVO stands for amperes, volts and ohms: the one instrument measures current, potential difference and resistance by switching between ranges.

q: A galvanometer gives full-scale deflection with a current of 50 μA. When it is made into a voltmeter, the voltmeter's resistance per volt of its range (its 'ohms per volt') is:
x: For a range V, the total resistance is V/Ig, so the resistance per volt is 1/Ig = 1/(50 × 10⁻⁶) = 20 000 Ω V⁻¹ = 20 kΩ V⁻¹. Writing μA as 10⁻⁵ A gives 2 kΩ V⁻¹.

q: A galvanometer of resistance 49 Ω is fitted with a shunt of 1 Ω. When a current of 5 A passes through the combination, the current through the galvanometer is:
x: The galvanometer and shunt share the same p.d., so the current divides inversely with resistance: Ig = 5 × 1/(49 + 1) = 0.1 A. The other 4.9 A passes through the shunt.

q: On the resistance scale of an ohmmeter (in an AVO meter), the zero-ohm mark is at the full-scale-deflection end of the scale because:
o: The meter's internal cell is disconnected when the probes are joined
A zero resistance draws no current from the cell
The pointer spring is weakest at full scale
With the probes joined directly, the circuit has least resistance and the largest current flows
x: The ohmmeter uses its own cell. With zero external resistance the current is largest, so the needle is set to full scale there and marked 0 Ω; larger resistances give smaller currents, so the scale runs backwards and is non-linear.

q: Two 10 kΩ resistors are connected in series across a 12 V supply of negligible internal resistance. A voltmeter of resistance 20 kΩ is connected across one of the resistors. Its reading is:
x: 10 kΩ in parallel with 20 kΩ is 20/3 kΩ ≈ 6.7 kΩ, in series with 10 kΩ: V = 12 × (20/3)/(50/3) = 12 × 0.4 = 4.8 V. An ideal voltmeter would read 6 V; 7.2 V is the p.d. across the other resistor.

q: A moving-coil galvanometer has a rectangular coil of 100 turns, 4 cm × 5 cm, in a radial magnetic field of 0.5 T. The suspension's torsion constant (couple per unit twist) is 2 × 10⁻⁵ N m rad⁻¹. The current that gives a deflection of 0.5 rad is:
x: At equilibrium NIAB = cθ. A = 20 cm² = 2 × 10⁻³ m², so I = cθ/(NAB) = (2 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.5)/(100 × 2 × 10⁻³ × 0.5) = 10⁻⁵/0.1 = 1 × 10⁻⁴ A. Leaving out θ gives 2 × 10⁻⁴ A.
